title: Research Questions and Hypotheses

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The null hypothesis is the sentence "nothing is going on here." A court starts from "not guilty" and only moves off that position when evidence is strong enough. Statistics does the same thing: it begins with "no difference" and discards that starting sentence only when the data would be very unlikely if it were true. That starting sentence is the null.

### Question 2

PICO is a template for asking a question a database can actually answer: who, what you try, what you weigh it against, and what you measure. Asking "does a warm compress help?" is like asking "is this shoe fast?" Fast compared with what, bare feet or a running shoe? Naming what you are comparing against is what turns a vague wondering into a question with a findable answer.

### Question 3

A usable hypothesis is a bet you could actually lose. "Something will happen tomorrow" is a bet no one can lose, so it carries no information. "Plants given fertilizer will grow taller than plants without it" can be checked with a ruler, and you might turn out to be wrong. That exposure to being wrong is exactly what makes a statement scientific, and it is called falsifiability.

### Question 4

Picture predicting a race. "The two runners will not finish together" claims a gap without naming a winner, which is nondirectional. "The runner in red finishes first" names the winner, which is directional. Both are genuine predictions, but the directional one commits to more and needs stronger prior evidence. Neither is the same as "they will tie," which is the null.

### Question 5

A question can be perfectly written and still be impossible to answer. If it requires 400 patients with a rare condition and you have one clinical site and one semester, the wording is not the problem, the logistics are. Feasibility is the reality check on people, time, money, and skill. Experienced researchers narrow the population or the outcome until the study can actually be carried out.

### Question 6

"Is music good for patients?" is like asking "is food healthy?" Which food, for whom, instead of what, and healthy measured how? Rewritten as "do adults awaiting outpatient surgery who listen to 20 minutes of slow instrumental music report lower anxiety scale scores than those who wait in silence," every piece is something you could count or score. Specificity is what makes a question answerable.

### Question 7

There are two ways to learn about an unfamiliar neighborhood. You can predict "the busiest corner is by the school" and go verify it, or you can walk every street and record what is actually there. Qualitative research is the second approach, so its questions stay open, such as "what is this experience like?" A prediction made beforehand would tell you where to look and quietly steer you past whatever you did not expect.

### Question 8

All four sentences concern the same study but play different roles. One names the winner (directional), one asserts sameness (the null), one asks (the research question), and one asserts a gap without naming a winner (nondirectional). Only the sentence that names the winner points in a specific direction, which is where the label "directional" comes from. Sorting them is a matter of checking the verb: predicts which way, denies, asks, or merely differs.

### Question 9

To build the null, do not flip the prediction over; erase it. The prediction was "spaced practice scores higher." Its null is not "spaced practice scores lower," which is simply the opposite prediction. It is "the two study methods produce the same scores." Think of a balance scale: the prediction says one pan drops, and the null says the scale stays level.

### Question 10

Suppose someone claims "attentive drivers are safer drivers." Before you can check it, you must decide what counts as attentive, perhaps a score on a distraction checklist, and what counts as safer, perhaps crashes per 10,000 miles. Until each fuzzy word has a stated way of being measured, no evidence could agree or disagree with the claim, so it remains an opinion rather than a hypothesis.

### Question 11

The question is "which commute route is fastest?" The hypothesis is the guess you record before you start timing: "the route past the park will be fastest." Committing first is what makes the timing a test. If you drove all the routes, saw the result, and only then announced what you had believed, you would have a story about the data rather than a test of a prediction.

### Question 12

Classify it with two checks. First, does it say which way the results go? Yes, "lower" and "shorter," so it is directional. Second, how many moving parts does it involve? Two intervention components and two outcomes, so it is complex rather than simple. It is like predicting not only that a team wins but that it wins by more goals and commits fewer fouls: one sentence carrying several distinct claims.
